shows.title: La familia elegida (The Chosen Family)
shows.description:
Argentine duo Leo Chiachio and Daniel Giannone have been sewing and embroidering self-portraits together since 2003, and this first solo show of theirs at Bendana | Pinel gathers works from that long-running project of self-representation as two queer men, life partners, and — as the exhibition's title makes explicit — a chosen family that also includes their three dachshunds. Made with needle, sewing machine, recycled fabric, dye, and thread, the pieces treat domesticity and self-portraiture as deliberately political acts, refusing the youthful, able-bodied image often expected of queer subjects and instead showing two artists aging together over two decades of work.

A more recent thread in their practice, developed during a residency in Bourges, brings in the stained glass of the city's cathedral — its lead lines and color fields — cross-referenced with the Argentine abstract movement Madi and especially the work of Yente (Eugenia Crenovich). Embroidered patterns drawn from these sources are layered onto fragments of 19th-century Jacquard-loom tapestry the artists gathered in France, then partly overprinted with silkscreened color, so each finished piece stacks several unrelated histories — Argentine, French, queer, textile-industrial — into a single surface.

The result is dense, personal, and unusually literal about its politics without losing its warmth: portraits of a family that doesn't fit inherited templates, built stitch by stitch over more than twenty years.

shows.title: Magnanrama: Media, Technologies, Identities, Networks Around Nathalie Magnan
shows.artist: Nathalie Magnan, with No Anger, Shu Lea Cheang, Cindy Coutant, Chloé Desmoineaux with Bobby Brim and Ada LaNerd, Guerrilla Girls, Barbara Hammer, Old Boys Network, Paper Tiger Television, Julia Scher, VNS Matrix
shows.description:
This group exhibition builds a collective portrait of Nathalie Magnan (1956–2016) — media theorist, filmmaker, cyberfeminist, and sailor — by surrounding her archive of films and documents with work by artists and collectives she worked alongside, taught, or influenced. Magnan spent three decades at the intersection of feminist and LGBTQIA+ activism and early networked technology, moving between academia, hacktivist circles, and video collectives in the US and France, and the show uses her biography as connective tissue rather than the sole subject.

The artists gathered here span four decades of cyberfeminist and media-critical practice: the Guerrilla Girls' anonymous, statistic-driven poster activism; the pioneering lesbian experimental filmmaker Barbara Hammer; the 1990s Berlin-based collective Old Boys Network and the Australian cyberpunk group VNS Matrix, both central to early cyberfeminism; the American video collective Paper Tiger Television, with whom Magnan made two films in Santa Cruz in the 1980s; and contemporary artists like No Anger, Cindy Coutant, and Chloé Desmoineaux (working with Bobby Brim and Ada LaNerd), whose current work on disability, hacking, and queer embodiment extends Magnan's questions into the present. Curated by Mathilde Belouali with Magnan's longtime partner Reine Prat, the exhibition combines archival photographs and ephemera with video installation and new commissions.

It's an unusually research-heavy, archive-driven show for a Paris art center, and a rare chance to encounter a figure — Magnan — who shaped cyberfeminist thought and media activism but remains far less known than the movements she helped build.

venue.name: Bétonsalon – Centre d'art et de recherche

shows.title: Éclipse
shows.description:
Timed to the nationwide Bicentenaire de la Photographie marking two hundred years since Nicéphore Niépce's first photographic image, this group show curated by Anne Favier asks what drawing has done with, and to, the photograph ever since. It's a smart, tightly argued premise: rather than treating photography and drawing as rival mediums, the exhibition tracks artists who use the pencil, the eraser and the mark-making hand to slow down, question or re-inhabit photographic images.

The roster splits roughly into two temperaments. On one side are artists who chase near-total photographic fidelity by hand — a historic body of work by Jean Olivier Hucleux anchors this strand, joined by Éric Manigaud, Mireille Blanc, Célia Muller and Daphné Le Sergent, all of whom labor to "re-draw" a photographic instant with obsessive, almost forensic patience. On the other side, artists like Léa Belooussovitch and Fabienne Ballandras use blurring, tracing and overlay to push source images toward abstraction or illegibility, worrying at the reliability of the photographic record itself, including media "shock photos."

A third group pushes past the flat picture altogether: Nicolas Daubanes' incandescent photograms, Jérémie Setton's interactive rig that makes the viewer complicit in developing an image, and Pascal Navarro's photosensitive works that reveal themselves slowly in the gallery light all treat drawing as a way of restaging photography's own founding chemistry — latent image, exposure, fixing. It's an ambitious, research-driven show, and a good one to catch early in its run given how much of it depends on light and time doing their work in the room.

shows.title: Saul Steinberg
shows.description:
Saul Steinberg spent a half-century drawing America back at itself — as a New Yorker cover artist, yes, but also as a genuinely strange visual philosopher who treated maps, alphabets, bureaucratic forms and building facades as material for satire and formal invention alike. This survey at Galerie Claude Bernard, a gallery with a long history of showing his work in Paris, gathers pieces spanning from the 1950s to the late 1970s.

Works on view trace his shifting preoccupations: "Times Square" (1953) catches his early fascination with the density and signage of American urban space; "The American Sphinx" (1964) shows him folding classical allegory into contemporary iconography; and "Lex Pax Lux" (1969) plays his taste for wordplay and mock-heraldic form against each other. A cover design made for The New Yorker in 1976 and the wry architectural fantasy "Eastern Federal Savings and Loan Association" (1978) round out a selection that moves fluidly between commercial illustration, gallery drawing and quiet institutional critique.

Steinberg is often filed under "cartoonist," a label he resisted and that undersells what's on view here: a draftsman as interested in Klee and Saul Bass as in gag panels, whose deadpan lines still read as some of the sharpest visual commentary on twentieth-century American life. For anyone who knows him only from magazine covers, this is a chance to see how much more supple and strange his line work gets in the gallery context.

shows.title: La traversée des Nuées
shows.description:
Léon Bongrain (1865–1948), nicknamed "le Mécano," is one of the rediscovery projects Loeve&Co built its program around: a self-taught painter who worked as a mechanic and came to art on his own terms, outside the academies and movements that usually organize art-historical narratives. The gallery published a monograph on him this year, and this show — its title translates as "The Crossing of the Clouds" — appears to gather paintings built around sky, atmosphere and passage.

Bongrain's biography and obscurity mean most visitors will be encountering this work for the first time, which is very much the point of Loeve&Co's program: rescuing overlooked French painters of the early twentieth century from the margins of the canon and giving them a proper, focused hang rather than a single line in a group survey.

Given the gallery's track record with similarly under-recognized figures, expect a show that leans on craft and atmosphere over art-world positioning — paintings to be looked at slowly, on their own terms, from an artist whose "mechanic" nickname suggests a hands-on, unpretentious relationship to his materials that the clouds-and-crossing title hints may have opened onto something more visionary.

shows.title: Festival of (in)gratitude
shows.description:
Walid Raad has spent nearly four decades turning the raw material of Lebanon's wars into elliptical, half-fictional archives, and this presentation — a world premiere staged with the Festival d'Automne — extends that project into new photographs, collages, drawings, texts, sculptures and video. Raad works less like a documentarian than a forger of plausible histories: his Atlas Group project invented a fictional foundation to hold "found" and "recovered" material from the Lebanese civil war, blurring the line between record and invention until the two become inseparable.

The show's animating events are the 1982–83 occupation of Lebanon, the massacres at Sabra and Chatila, and the PLO's exile to Tunis, but Raad treats these as starting points for a much wider drift across geographies and time — from Beirut to Tunis to Ljubljana — that also takes in the history of art-making in the Arab world. True to his hybrid method, the artist himself leads guided walkthroughs of the installation, appearing as archivist and storyteller rather than didactic guide, mixing invented, inherited and discovered stories in the same breath.

Presented in the Écuries space at CENTQUATRE as part of the Saison Méditerranée, the exhibition is free and bilingual (French/English), with Raad's own performed tours running most afternoons and evenings throughout the run — worth timing a visit around, since the work is built to be narrated as much as looked at.

shows.title: L'Ergriffenheit (A State of Being Seized)
shows.description:
Patrick Van Caeckenbergh's ninth solo show with the gallery takes its title from the German word for the state of being seized or overwhelmed — the feeling the Belgian artist locates in childhood play, where instinct tips over into a kind of poetic worldview. Van Caeckenbergh has spent decades building an idiosyncratic cosmology out of drawing, sculpture, taxidermy-like assemblage and obsessive collecting, treating the studio as a cabinet of curiosities where natural history, folklore and personal mythology are catalogued side by side.

Known for works that resemble scientific specimens gone feral — nests, hives, and diagrammatic trees rendered with the fastidiousness of an eccentric naturalist — Van Caeckenbergh uses that same sensibility here to think about wonder as a reflex rather than an achievement, something closer to a child's unmediated absorption in the natural world than to adult contemplation. Expect the dense, handmade, slightly obsessive vocabulary that has made his work a fixture of exhibitions from the Villa Médicis to Kunstmuseum Wolfsburg.

The opening, on Sunday September 13, doubles as a communal meal: the artist is preparing and serving soup himself, in keeping with a practice that treats hospitality and domestic ritual as extensions of the work itself.

venue.name: In Situ - fabienne leclerc
venue.address: 43 Rue de la Commune de Paris

shows.title: Faire place au monde (Making Room for the World)
shows.description:
Curated by Chương-Đài Võ, Charles Esche and Federica Chiocchetti, this group exhibition takes the Cité internationale des arts itself — a residency founded after the Second World War on the premise that artistic exchange could forge bonds nation-states had failed to sustain — as its subject and starting point. Sixteen artists from fifteen countries, all former or current residents spanning more than two decades (2003 to today), contribute work that interrogates what "internationalism" actually costs and confers.

The show's throughline is the uneven reality of cross-border artistic life: for some participating artists, mobility is a daily negotiation shadowed by displacement and the search for hospitality; for others, it is opportunity shot through with dependency. Works on view include Gustavo Ciríaco and João Gonçalo Lopes's Caravanserá, staging the caravan and carnival as models of exchange and welcome; Young Joo Lee's oil painting The Congress; and Taysir Batniji's spare, charged sculpture of a suitcase filled with sand. Other artists in the show include Louidgi Beltrame, Emma Charrin, Kari Ikonen, Olia Fedorova, Thomas Henriksson, Ola Hassanain, Himat M. Ali, Zbyněk Baladrán, Hussein Nassereddine, Cristina Escobar, Gluklya, and Wendie Zahibo.

Given the Cité's own history and self-conception as "a city within a city" suspending national hierarchies, the exhibition doubles as institutional self-examination — asking whether a place built to transcend borders can escape reproducing the very asymmetries of power and access it was meant to dissolve. It's an ambitious, research-driven survey for a venue better known for open studios than curated group shows, and worth catching for the range of practices and geographies it brings together in one space.

shows.title: Unfinished thinking: Paintings and Social Maps
shows.dates_note: Venue's own page lists only "Opening October 19, 2026" with no closing date given.
shows.description:
Oscar Murillo returns to David Zwirner's Paris space with a new body of paintings and "social maps" — the loosely gridded, collaboratively inflected canvases that have become a signature of his practice since he began inviting participants worldwide to contribute marks to shared surfaces. Murillo, born in Colombia and raised between La Paila and London, has built a body of work around themes of migration, labor, and collective identity, often layering paint, oil stick, and thread into surfaces that feel worked-over and lived-in rather than composed.

The artist's own fragmented statement accompanying the show — invoking speed, geography, labor, and a "sea of marks" spanning Colombia, Cameroon, Ivory Coast, the Philippines, the UK, and Poland — signals a continuation of his interest in globalized labor and diasporic experience as raw material for abstraction. Expect large-scale canvases where gesture, repetition, and accumulated color stand in for the "profound statements" and "scars of people" he describes, work that resists easy legibility in favor of density and duration.

Coming right on the heels of the gallery's 40th-anniversary group show at the same address, this solo exhibition gives Murillo — one of the more prominent painters of his generation — a full-scale Paris platform to build out his ongoing inquiry into what collective, transnational mark-making can look like.

shows.title: Mes Dalton
shows.artist: Pierre Ardouvin, Pierre Besson, Michel Blazy, Lilian Bourgeat, Anne Brégeaut, Céline Cléron, François Curlet, Michael Dans, François Dufeil, Sammy Engramer, Makiko Furuichi, Michel Gouéry, Sébastien Gouju, Laurent Le Deunff, Jacques Lizène, Vincent Mauger, Anita Molinero, Daniel Nadaud, Bruno Peinado, David Posth-Kohler, Céleste Richard-Zimmermann, Elsa Sahal, Michaela Sanson-Braun, Christophe Terlinden, Didier Trénet, Clémence van Lunen, Stéphane Vigny
shows.description:
Twenty-seven artists fill Loevenbruck's rue Jacques-Callot space for this group show built around a single act of friendship: curator Bertrand Godot, after thirty years running the exhibition program at the Chapelle du Genêteil in Château-Gontier, was abruptly let go last year, and "Mes Dalton" gathers the artists he championed there across three decades as a gesture of loyalty and reckoning. The title borrows from the Lucky Luke outlaw brothers — a nod to affectionate, slightly disreputable kinship rather than any painterly theme.

The installation is the real subject: small works sit directly on the floor near the entrance, and pieces grow progressively larger and higher as visitors move through the space, an ascent Godot has described as a blunt metaphor for social hierarchy, where the small get consumed by the big. It closes on a single wall-mounted work, François Curlet's triptych of photographs taken for a 1987 issue of Playboy, which stands apart from the rest of the show like a screen backdrop.

Expect a wide range of materials and temperaments — ceramic and resin figures from Elsa Sahal and Michel Gouéry, cast and constructed objects from Bruno Peinado and Vincent Mauger, folk-inflected assemblage from Daniel Nadaud, and sculptural gardens from Stéphane Vigny — reflecting Godot's long-standing interest in artists working outside fashionable centers. It's less a survey of a movement than a portrait of one curator's eye, assembled by the gallerist who invited him to make it.

venue.name: Galerie Loevenbruck
hours: Tue - Sat 11am to 7pm and by appointment

shows.title: Petrol M*other Paris
shows.description:
This solo show brings the Vienna-based painter Ashley Hans Scheirl to Loevenbruck's 6, rue Jacques-Callot space. Scheirl, who won the Oskar Kokoschka Prize (Austria's top honor for a living artist) in 2026 jointly with Jakob Lena Knebl — whose own solo show opens the same night around the corner at Loevenbruck's second space — has spent four decades moving between painting, film, and performance, with work that pushes queer and trans embodiment into deliberately garish, glossy, and unstable pictorial territory.

Since the 1980s Scheirl's paintings have mixed airbrushed surfaces, collage, and sly appropriation of pulp and advertising imagery to unsettle fixed ideas of gender and desire. Expect large-scale canvases that trade in slippery, mutating bodies and a visual language closer to B-movie posters or music videos than to gallery painting's usual reserve — an appropriate register for an artist who has always treated identity as a costume to be tried on rather than a fact to be defended.

The exhibition's title, playing on "mother" and "petrol," hints at the kind of blunt, materially charged wordplay that runs through Scheirl's practice. Coming right on the heels of major institutional attention (a current solo at Vienna's Belvedere 21), this is a chance to see new work from an artist finally getting wider recognition after decades of influence on younger queer and feminist painters.

venue.name: Galerie Loevenbruck
hours: Tue - Sat 11am to 7pm and by appointment

shows.title: Waiting for the Sound of Thunder
shows.description:
Jakob Lena Knebl takes over Loevenbruck's second space at 12, rue Jacques-Callot with a solo exhibition that continues the artist's long-running practice of building immersive, theatrical environments out of furniture, fashion, found objects, and her own sculptural figures. Knebl, who represented Austria at the Venice Biennale in 2022 and shared this year's Oskar Kokoschka Prize with Ashley Hans Scheirl (whose own show opens the same evening at Loevenbruck's other address), treats the exhibition space itself as a kind of stage set, mixing camp, desire, and domestic kitsch into installations that resist any single reading of gender or taste.

Recent work has included reclining or hovering figures built from mannequins, textiles, and everyday furnishings — objects that feel plucked from a department store display and recomposed into something stranger and more erotic. Expect a similarly hybrid, maximalist installation here, continuing threads seen this year in her exhibition at the Marmorschlössl in Bad Ischl.

Knebl's work rewards slow looking: what first reads as decor or humor usually turns out to be doing careful work around visibility, self-fashioning, and the body. This is a rare chance to see a substantial new installation from her in Paris.

shows.title: Demande à la poussière (Ask the Dust): TETHYS
shows.description:
Ségolène Kan spent time in Mangystau, a wind-scoured limestone plateau in western Kazakhstan on the shore of the Caspian, and this show — curated by Olya Vesselova — is built entirely from what she brought back: watercolor-and-earth landscapes that reduce the region to its essentials of horizon, sky, and a receding road. The series takes its title, TETHYS, from the ancient sea that once covered the region 190 million years ago, and each canvas repeats a near-identical composition — a thin band of ground, an enormous sky, a road disappearing at one edge — as if testing how much variation a single formula for infinity can hold.

Technically the works are built from wet-on-wet watercolor overlaid with pigment and earth, letting the paint pool and bleed before a denser line is drawn on top once it dries — a combination the gallery links to Japanese sumi-e ink painting, American watercolorists like Andrew Wyeth, and the palette-knife density of late Van Gogh. The palette stays narrow throughout: ochre and burnt sienna standing in for the sun-scoured ground, cobalt for a sky that seems to remember the water that used to be there.

Kan, a Paris-born painter who trained in the abstract painting studio at the Beaux-Arts de Paris, works at the boundary between abstraction and landscape, and this body of work pushes that further than her earlier series — the geology of Mangystau's cliffs and canyons becomes almost the whole subject, with human presence reduced to a road and nothing else. It's a quiet, contemplative show built around a single, patiently repeated idea.

shows.title: ŒuVreS réCEnteS (Recent Works)
shows.description:
Jutta Koether has spent four decades treating painting as an argument rather than a settled medium — her canvases layer gestural abstraction, art-historical quotation, and a distinctly punk sensibility inherited from her years as a critic and musician in Cologne's 1980s scene. This show of recent work, its title rendered in the artist's own idiosyncratic mixed capitalization, continues her ongoing interrogation of what a painting is allowed to do once you stop treating the canvas as a neutral rectangle.

Koether's paintings tend to fold in references to older art (Poussin, Titian, and her long-running engagement with erotic and religious imagery) alongside passages of pure abstract mark-making, often staged with theatrical, stage-set devices — mirrors, structures, painted supports that intrude into the viewer's space. Expect a show that resists a single reading and instead accumulates meaning through friction between styles and eras.

As one of the key figures to emerge from the Cologne painting scene and a longtime contributor to art criticism and experimental music, Koether occupies an unusual position: a painter whose work is inseparable from a broader critical practice. This exhibition offers a compact, current view into where that practice stands now.

shows.title: Nick Mauss
shows.description:
Nick Mauss works across painting, drawing, sculpture, and installation, often treating a gallery less as a set of walls to hang things on than as a stage to choreograph — his shows have long drawn on the history of decorative arts, dance, and early-twentieth-century modernism as material to be reanimated rather than cited. This self-titled exhibition, running concurrently with Jutta Koether's show in the gallery's other space, continues that hybrid practice.

Mauss's work frequently blurs the line between figure and ornament: hazy, atmospheric paintings and works on paper sit alongside sculptural elements — mirrored surfaces, vitrines, furniture-like forms — that reframe the paintings as part of a larger environment rather than isolated objects. His long-standing interest in the history of exhibition-making itself (he has staged projects that excavate archival material from past decades of French and German art institutions) gives even his most abstract-looking paintings a research-driven undercurrent.

Having exhibited at institutions from the Whitney to the Kunsthalle Basel, Mauss brings a curatorial sensibility to his own installations, and this show promises the kind of considered, atmosphere-first hang that has become his signature.

shows.title: Lucky Jim
shows.description:
Seven years after his last show at the gallery, James Barnor — now 97, one of the great chroniclers of Ghanaian modernity and the Black British diaspora — returns with a selection of previously unseen prints centered on self-portraiture and self-staging. Rather than tracing his career chronologically, the show follows him as a recurring character within his own vast archive: a young father posing with his infant son at a christening in Accra, a studio portrait from the 1950s in a striped suit, a picture of him in kente cloth beside an "England" road sign taken by a close friend during his London years.

Barnor's career spans pre-independence Ghana, London during the era of Windrush-generation nightlife and fashion photography, and a return to Accra in the 1970s where he ran a busy portrait studio and shot advertising work (including a well-known Agip calendar series). What ties this particular selection together is the photographer turning the camera on himself — a set of images the gallery describes as amounting to the emotional core of the archive, surfacing only now after years of cataloguing and research.

The show's timing is not incidental: it opens shortly before Ibrahim Mahama's exhibition at the Fondation Cartier, which draws on Barnor's own photographs and underscores the two artists' shared interest in Ghana, memory and the act of archiving. For anyone who has followed Barnor's rediscovery over the past decade, this is a chance to see a more intimate, self-reflective side of a photographer usually known for documenting everyone but himself.

shows.title: Alone Together
shows.description:
For her second solo show at Galerie Claire Gastaud's Paris space, Milène Sanchez presents a new body of paintings built up in glazes of oil on canvas — a slow, layered technique with roots in early Renaissance painting, here put toward loose, gestural abstraction. The paintings followed a trip to New York where Sanchez spent time with the work of Joan Mitchell, Lee Krasner, Helen Frankenthaler and Elaine de Kooning, and something of Abstract Expressionism's physical urgency has clearly filtered into her own handling of paint.

Sanchez, born in 1997 and trained at ESAD Saint-Étienne, works in a register where the body and its gestures matter as much as any fixed image — she has spoken of not stopping when a canvas seems to be failing, but pushing through to find something unplanned. Traces, light and what she calls "vestiges" recur across the individual canvases, which she considers independent but bound together as a single ongoing account of her own experience.

It's an interesting show to catch for anyone tracking how a younger generation of European painters is metabolizing the legacy of American gestural abstraction — Sanchez has been gaining institutional traction quickly, with recent presentations at FRAC Auvergne, the Fondation CAB in Brussels and a solo show at ICICLE Culture Space in Shanghai.

shows.title: Cy Twombly: Sperlonga 1959
shows.description:
In the summer of 1959, newly settled in Italy, Cy Twombly spent a season in the small coastal village of Sperlonga and produced roughly thirty works on paper that mark one of the pivotal turns in his career. This exhibition, devoted entirely to that group, reconstructs a specific moment: the blinding Mediterranean light, the whitewashed houses, and the proximity of Emperor Tiberius's villa, where a cache of first-century sculptures inspired by the Odyssey had been unearthed just two years earlier.

The drawings themselves are spare almost to the point of emptiness, built from a few marks, numbers, circles and near-cartographic notations set against wide unworked fields of paper. Rather than depicting the sea or coastline directly, Twombly lets blank space and a scatter of gesture stand in for horizon and light, opening what curator Kirk Varnedoe, writing for Twombly's 1994 MoMA retrospective, called a distinctly landscape-like space within his work. Thick impasto and loose brushwork sit next to almost weightless pencil lines.

The Sperlonga works occupy a hinge point in Twombly's development, the moment his engagement with landscape, myth, and the classical past crystallized into a vocabulary he would keep refining for another five decades. For a gallery that gave Twombly his first show in 1971, this is a focused, scholarly presentation of an unusually tight body of work rather than a career survey, and it rewards visitors willing to slow down in front of drawings whose reticence is exactly the point.

shows.title: Les Fous d'En Face
shows.description:
Elmgreen & Dragset have spent three decades turning white-cube galleries into abandoned subway stations, defunct swimming pools, and fake boutiques, using architectural reconfiguration to needle at the systems, institutional, domestic, urban, that quietly organize public and private life. Les Fous d'En Face ("The Madmen Across the Way") brings that practice to the gallery's Paris rooms for a new solo presentation following major recent outings at the Musée d'Orsay and the Städel Museum.

True to form with this Berlin-based duo, expect the show to treat the gallery itself as raw material as much as a neutral container, continuing their long interest in displacement and reconfiguration, taking familiar objects, architectural elements or display conventions and shifting them just enough to expose the assumptions built into them. Their sculptures and installations, sometimes called "Powerless Structures," tend to combine deadpan humor with a sharper commentary on class, institutional authority, and the theater of public space.

With a title that plays on ideas of madness and surveillance, seeing versus being seen from across a divide, this promises another characteristically wry, spatially inventive intervention from two artists who have made a career out of unsettling the white cube from the inside.

shows.title: Tolika Mtoliki
shows.artist: Nicholas Hlobo, Bulumko Mbete, Kagiso Patrick Mautloa, Mankebe Seakgoe, Frans Thoka, Benjamin Stanwix & Xhanti Zwelendaba
shows.description:
Tolika Mtoliki gathers six South African artists around the idea that translation isn't only linguistic — that objects, materials and gestures can carry stories, memory and knowledge across contexts just as words do. The title itself comes from the isiXhosa/isiZulu word for "to translate," and the show uses it loosely to link very different practices: Nicholas Hlobo's stitched-together sculptures of ribbon, leather, wood and rubber offcuts, which probe masculinity and isiXhosa identity; Bulumko Mbete's textile and beadwork pieces drawn from women's craft traditions treated as a form of indigenous archive; and Kagiso Patrick Mautloa's assemblages of urban found objects built up with wood, cement and foam.

Frans Thoka works with the prison blanket as both material and subject, addressing incarceration, displacement and marginalization, while Mankebe Seakgoe's works sit between drawing and script — inscriptions that resemble writing without settling into legibility. Xhanti Zwelendaba and Benjamin Stanwix close the circle with reworked archival images of South African landscapes woven onto ikhukho, a traditional hand-woven reed or grass mat, questioning how histories get preserved, passed down and retold.

It's a tightly curated group show that leans into MAGNIN-A's long-standing focus on contemporary African art, with textile, sculpture and mixed media doing most of the talking rather than painting — a good entry point for anyone whose sense of the gallery is built around its Congolese and West African painters.

shows.title: Entre temps
shows.description:
Leandro Erlich brings his signature brand of perceptual trickery to Xippas Paris with a suite of works built around memory, obsolescence and the passage of time. The show opens with "Pulled by the Roots," a house wrenched from the ground and suspended in mid-air, then moves through "Draft-Bazza," a series of vintage typewriters entombed in sand and displayed under glass domes like archaeological relics of a pre-digital age.

The centerpiece is "Classroom," a life-size reconstruction of a 1970s schoolroom that Erlich first developed for the Mori Art Museum in Tokyo and here presents in France for the first time, in partnership with Galleria Continua. Viewers approach through a darkened corridor and look in through glass at desks, a blackboard and dust-covered furniture, only to see their own reflection ghosted into the abandoned room — merging with strangers' silhouettes as though everyone were seated together at the old desks.

Erlich, an Argentine artist known internationally for illusionistic, participatory installations (his swimming pool and building-facade works have become widely recognizable), continues here his long-running interest in architecture as a vessel for shared memory. The classroom motif also carries a pointed contemporary note: declining birth rates in France have shuttered many real classrooms, and the installation asks what is lost, socially and personally, when such spaces disappear.

Coming on the heels of Erlich's major outdoor presentation at the Grand Palais this past summer, this gallery show offers a more intimate, object-based counterpoint — a chance to see the mechanics of his illusions at close range rather than across a monumental public space.

venue.name: Xippas
venue.address: 108 rue Vieille du Temple, 75003 Paris, France
